headline: Massachusetts Question 7 would override local lot-size rules for some starter homes
dek: The Nov. 3 referendum would allow single-family homes on qualifying 5,000-square-foot lots, with supporters promising more housing and municipal officials warning about local control and infrastructure limits.
body: Massachusetts voters will decide Nov. 3 whether to make it easier to build some single-family homes on smaller lots, putting a statewide answer to local zoning rules before the electorate as the state struggles with high housing costs and limited supply. Question 7 is one of nine binding statewide questions on the 2026 ballot. The official [Secretary of the Commonwealth ballot summary](https://www.sec.state.ma.us/divisions/elections/research-and-statistics/2026-ballot-questions.htm) says a yes vote would allow a single-family home in a residentially zoned area when the lot is at least 5,000 square feet, has at least 50 feet along a street or public way and has access to public water and sewer.

The proposal would change who sets the baseline for those homes. Under current practice, cities and towns can establish minimum lot sizes that are often larger than 5,000 square feet. Question 7 would amend the state zoning framework so a qualifying home could be built without a special permit, according to [WBUR’s Oct. 7 explanation](https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/07/massachusetts-election-ballot-question-7-starter-homes-small-lots). The measure would still let local governments reasonably regulate details such as height, parking, open space, distance from neighboring buildings and short-term rentals.

That means the question is not a promise that every eligible parcel will produce a house, nor is it a statewide affordable-housing mandate. It is a change in the set of homes that could be considered as-of-right where the land and utilities meet the stated conditions. Boston would be outside the measure because its zoning system is not governed by Chapter 40A, the state law that Question 7 would amend. The Massachusetts General Court’s [Chapter 40A page](https://malegislature.gov/Laws/GeneralLaws/PartI/TitleVII/Chapter40A) identifies the statute as the Commonwealth’s main municipal-zoning framework.

The likely scale of construction is the largest unresolved practical question. The Tufts University Center for State Policy Analysis estimates that the measure would lead to about 750 new homes a year, with a plausible range of 350 to 1,200. Its [analysis](https://cspa.tufts.edu/node/2511) projects an increase of roughly 15% in single-family construction and about 5% in overall housing development. It also estimates that roughly 200,000 parcels would gain new construction options, with the biggest building increase likely in suburbs, particularly Boston-area communities that already have sewer infrastructure and lots large enough to divide.

Those figures are notably more restrained than the estimate offered by the ballot campaign. WBUR reported that the campaign’s analysis projected 2,200 to 5,700 net new homes per year. The difference reflects assumptions about how many property owners would pursue a project, how many lots could actually be split and how much demand would translate into completed construction. Neither estimate is a guarantee, and neither says where a particular house would be built or what it would cost.

Supporters describe the proposal as a way to create more modest homes for buyers who are priced out of the existing market. Legalize Starter Homes chair Andrew Mikula told WBUR that large minimum lots can push builders toward bigger, more expensive houses because the cost of acquiring land has to be recovered. Abundant Housing Massachusetts executive director Jesse Kanson-Benanav said smaller homes could help first-time buyers and older residents who want to downsize without leaving their communities. Those are arguments about the measure’s potential; the ballot text itself does not require a home built under Question 7 to be sold at a below-market price.

The Massachusetts Municipal Association has raised a different concern: that the initiative would remove decisions from local officials who understand a community’s infrastructure, finances and physical limits. The association’s executive director, Adam Chapdelaine, told WBUR that the presence of a sewer and water pipe does not necessarily mean a system can handle additional demand. He also argued that the wording would permit market-rate or luxury construction, rather than guaranteeing starter homes. The measure’s supporters and critics therefore agree that housing supply is a problem but disagree over whether a uniform state rule is the right tool.

Water and sewer access would narrow the measure’s reach. WBUR reported that large areas of western Massachusetts, the Cape, the South Shore and parts of the North Shore do not have public sewer service, making them less likely to benefit directly even if their lots are otherwise large enough. The Tufts analysis likewise expects the strongest effect in suburbs with existing infrastructure. In practice, Question 7’s impact would be shaped by which parcels have utilities, how local rules are written and whether owners and builders decide that projects make financial sense.

If voters approve the question, the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities would write guidance or regulations for implementation, while municipalities would retain authority over the listed design and use controls. The state’s official summary says a no vote would leave the law unchanged relative to building single-family homes. The immediate choice is thus between a common statewide floor for qualifying lots and continued local control over minimum lot-size rules. The housing shortage gives the referendum urgency, but the competing estimates and infrastructure conditions mean the result would be measured over years, not by an instant statewide surge in construction.
